deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the draft of §6 of Riemann's 1851 Inauguraldissertation ('Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'). The section introduces cross-cuts (Querschnitte) and simply connected surfaces in order to define the order of connectivity. The previous page defined a cross-cut as a simple arc running through the interior from one boundary point to another. A connected surface is simply connected ('einfach zusammenhängend') if every cross-cut disconnects it.

LEHRSATZ I. Claim: a simply connected surface A is split by any cross-cut ab into two pieces, and each piece is simply connected.
Proof by contradiction. Suppose one piece P is not disconnected by some cross-cut cd of P. Restore the junction of the two pieces along part of ab, choosing the part by where the endpoints of cd lie:
(i) neither c nor d lies on ab: rejoin along all of ab;
(ii) c lies on ab: rejoin along the part cb;
(iii) both c and d lie on ab: rejoin along the part of ab between them.
In each case the result is a connected surface. Implicitly (my gloss), it is A cut along one cross-cut: in (i) that cross-cut is cd itself, in (ii) it is cd extended along ca, in (iii) it is a–c, then the arc cd, then d–b. This contradicts the simple connectivity of A.

LEHRSATZ II. Setting:
- n1 cross-cuts q1 cut T into a system T1 of m1 simply connected pieces;
- n2 cross-cuts q2 cut T into a system T2 of m2 pieces (not necessarily simply connected).
Claim: n2 − m2 ≤ n1 − m1.

Step 1. Any q2 not lying entirely in the q1-lines gives one or more cross-cuts q2' of T1. Their endpoints are of two kinds:
(1) The 2n2 endpoints of the q2. Exclude those lying on the q1-system:
- ν2 = number of times an end-piece of a q2 coincides with a middle piece of a q1;
- ν3 = number of times an end-piece of a q2 coincides with an end-piece of a q1.
This kind contributes 2n2 − ν2 − ν3 endpoints.
(2) Interior points of a q2 where it enters a middle point of a q1. Let μ count how often lines of the two systems meet or separate, so an isolated common point counts twice. Exclude those points where the q2 is already on another q1, i.e. where an end of a q1 lies on the q2; their number is ν1. This kind contributes μ − ν1 endpoints.

Step 2. The two kinds together cover all endpoints, each once. Each q2' has two ends, so
#q2' = (2n2 − ν2 − ν3 + μ − ν1)/2 = n2 + s,
where s = (μ − ν1 − ν2 − ν3)/2 (s defined implicitly; making it explicit is mine).

Step 3. Symmetrically, the q1 form cross-cuts q1' of T2, and
#q1' = (2n1 − ν1 − ν3 + μ − ν2)/2 = n1 + s.
The s is the same in both counts because the expression is symmetric in the two systems.

Step 4 (completed on the next page). T1 cut by the q2' and T2 cut by the q1' give the same surface, namely T cut by both systems. By repeated use of Lehrsatz I, the m1 simply connected pieces of T1 become m1 + n2 + s pieces. Each cross-cut raises the number of pieces by at most 1, so m1 + n2 + s ≤ m2 + n1 + s. Hence n2 − m2 ≤ n1 − m1.

Consequence (next page): n − m is the same for all dissections into simply connected pieces. This is the 'Ordnung des Zusammenhangs' (connectivity number).
errors: No arithmetic errors: both counts are correct, and the symmetric formula gives the same s for both systems.

Implicit, unproved assumptions: (a) the two systems meet only finitely often (general position), which is needed for μ and the ν's to be finite; (b) the bookkeeping of degenerate cases (end-pieces lying on boundary points, overlapping segments) is asserted rather than proved. This is the well-known lack of rigour in Riemann's connectivity argument, later criticised and repaired (e.g. by Tonelli, Weyl and others).

Lehrsatz I silently uses that the rejoined surface really arises from A by a single cross-cut, i.e. that the composite arc is simple. Cases (ii) and (iii) need cd to meet ab only at its endpoints, which holds because cd lies in the piece.

results.what: A simply connected surface is cut by any cross-cut into two simply connected pieces
results.modern_name: Cutting a disc along a proper arc gives two discs (Jordan-type separation lemma)

results.what: n2 − m2 ≤ n1 − m1 when the first system of cuts produces simply connected pieces; hence n − m is invariant
results.modern_name: Invariance of the connectivity number (equivalent to invariance of the Euler characteristic / first Betti number of a bordered surface)

results.what: Counting the endpoints of the induced cross-cuts via μ, ν1, ν2, ν3
results.modern_name: Combinatorial intersection count in the proof of connectivity invariance

deep.surprise_reason: This is essentially the text of §6 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation (Lehrsätze I and II on cross-cuts and the order of connectivity). It is well known and credited to him; the draft only shows minor wording variants.

checkable.sympy: n1,n2,mu,v1,v2,v3=symbols('n1 n2 mu v1 v2 v3'); s=(mu-v1-v2-v3)/2; simplify((2*n2-v2-v3+mu-v1)/2-(n2+s))==0
checkable.asserts: The number of q2' cross-cuts equals n2 + s
The number of q1' cross-cuts equals n1 + s, with the same s
The inequality m1+n2+s ≤ m2+n1+s is equivalent to n2−m2 ≤ n1−m1

transcription_corrections: Line 2 opens with a struck or uncertain siglum ('II.' or 'A.'), written beneath the underlined heading 'Lehrsatz I'; 'II[?]' should be marked as a deletion or uncertain siglum, not as content.
'auseinander andergehen' is a line-break duplication; read 'auseinandergehen' (auseinan-/dergehen).
In case 2 the manuscript reads 'jeder mittlere Punkt eines Querschnitts q2, in welchem er in einen mittleren Punkt einer Linie q1 eintritt'; this is consistent with the transcription.
'Fläche [-System-] T1' and 'Fläche [-System-] T2': 'System' is struck in favour of 'Fläche' (rendered 'Fläche' in the image as 'der Fläche'); correct as given.
